tldr: ReSearch is a novel framework that trains LLMs to reason with external search via reinforcement learning (GRPO) without any supervised reasoning data, treating search operations as integral parts of the reasoning chain.
contributions: Proposes ReSearch, a framework using reinforcement learning to train LLMs to reason with search from scratch without supervised data on reasoning steps
Demonstrates effectiveness across multiple multi-hop QA benchmarks by training on both 7B and 32B Qwen2.5 models, showing strong generalizability from training on only one dataset (MuSiQue)
Shows that ReSearch naturally elicits advanced reasoning capabilities such as reflection and self-correction during RL without relying on pre-defined heuristics
methods: The authors propose ReSearch, which uses Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to train LLMs where rollouts contain text-based thinking (<think>), search queries (<search>), and retrieval results (<result>). Search operations are masked in loss calculation so the policy is not biased toward retrieved tokens. A rule-based reward function combines F1 score for answer correctness with a format reward for proper tag usage. Training was conducted from scratch on Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-32B (both base and instruction-tuned variants) using only the MuSiQue training set (19,938 samples, 2 epochs) with Wikipedia-based retrieval via FlashRAG and E5-base-v2 retriever.
results: ReSearch achieves significant absolute improvements over baselines: average improvement of 15.81% in exact match and 17.56% in LLM-as-a-judge for 7B models, and 14.82% in exact match and 15.46% in LLM-as-a-judge for 32B models, across HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, and Bamboogle benchmarks. Training from instruction-tuned models further improved performance over base models. Response length and number of search operations both increased during training, indicating the model learned iterative multi-hop search behavior.
limitations: Training was conducted on only one dataset (MuSiQue), though generalization to other benchmarks was demonstrated. The method relies on a simple rule-based reward function. The paper notes that collecting labeled reasoning data with search for supervised fine-tuning is impractical due to costs, but does not explore alternative reward designs or larger-scale training datasets.
